BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, choices, and challenge. 19 terms about game design from meaningful play and agency to risk, trade-offs, fairness, luck, balance, and downtime. With the exact term you can tell a play-dester or an AI coding agent what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for Bear. Newcomers often say a hard game is an unfair game. It is not. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is. Fairness is whether the player can learn from losing. A game can be very hard and still fair. This film goes through 19 terms on choices and challenge, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Five labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 19 terms about game design in four groups. The first group is choices that matter. Meaningful play, both descriptive and evaluative, meaningful choice and agency. These terms ask whether the player's action means something.

B0102.heard: The second group is kinds of interesting decision. Risk versus reward, trade off, persistence, situational choice, personalization, and unit differentiation. These terms say what makes one decision more interesting than another.

B0103.heard: The third group is the challenge, frustration, difficulty, fairness and luck and skill. These terms ask how hard a game is and whether the player can learn from losing.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Balance and Waiting. Balance, Rock Paper Sisters, Downtime and Probability. These terms ask whether every option and every turn is worth taking.

B0201.heard: A red bowl of flies across and hits a block of ice and the ice shatters. Meaningful play means the player acts and the game responds in a way that matters. Descriptive play is the first half of that, an action followed by a clear response the player sees at once. For example, in a platformer you build, the player stomps an enemy, it flattens with a squash sound, and the way ahead is clear.

B0202.heard: Now a chain of five boxes runs from Throw Bola to finish game, with a red arc joining the ends. Evaluative play is the player stepping back to ask why an action matters to the whole game. Here the one throw is four steps from finishing. For example, a player realizes that the key picked up in the first room is what opens the door before the goal flag, so the detour mattered.

B0203.heard: Two lines branched through three forks. Agency also called autonomy means the player takes control of how the game is played. Three forks with two ways each make eight possible routes, two times two times two, and the red player and the black player finish the same level by different ones. For example, give your level a high path over the spikes in a low path under them, and let each player decide which way to go.

B0301.heard: Bars of points, risk versus reward means a harder or riskier action pays more, and the player weighs the factors before trying it. In this made-up example, an invader is worth 10 to 30 points, while the UFO, which is harder to hit, gives 50 to 150 and 300 on the 23rd shot. For example, put a coin on a narrow ledge right above the spikes and make it worth more than the coins on the safe path.

B0302.heard: Three situations each scored as reward minus cost. A meaningful choice changes what happens, and the player has to think about it. In this made-up example, the same UFO scores plus 25.5 when the player is behind, minus 17 when the invaders are near, and plus 3 on the last life. For example, a player on one heart has to think hard about jumping for a bonus coin over a pit, while a player on full health may simply go for it.

B0401.heard: A score line over time, a trade off means giving up one thing to get another. In this made up example, the gray player scores a steady 10 points a second. The red player gives up a ship at 8 seconds, rescues it for dual fire, then scores 20 seconds and pulls ahead after 18 seconds. For example, offer the player a heavy shield that blocks every hit but makes them jump lower.

B0402.heard: Eight moments in a stage and four power pellets. Persistence means the player has to carry the consequences of a choice for a set time. Here all four pellets go in the first four moments, the red boxes, so at the big group of ghosts none are left until the next stage. For example, if the player spends all of the levels bombs on the first few enemies, the boss at the end has to be fought without them.

B0501.heard: A grid of enemies sordid by how they move and how they attack. Unit differentiation, also called orthogonal unit differentiation, means each enemy type does something different which forces the player to prioritize. The imp charges and its fireballs can be dodged, the cacodemon stays back and the shotgun guy never misses. For example, give your platformer one enemy that rushes the player along a ledge and another that throws rocks from far away.

B0502.heard: Bars now rank the threat you cannot dodge. Situational choice means the same choice is better or worse depending on the situation the player is in. In this made up example the shotgun guy deals 10 damage a second that cannot be dodged. The Kakodemon 3 and the imp 2.5 so the shotgun guy goes first. For example with a turret and a walking enemy in the room break the turret first but with walkers alone jumping over them may be better.

B0601.heard: Three rows of decisions read for a risky pick and black for a safe one. Personalization means players build their own play style from the decisions they make. All three face the same 20 decisions and each chooses a different mix. For example, in a level with an optional enemy in every room, one player fights each one while another sneaks past them all and both reach the goal.

B0602.heard: Now each row is counted in this simulated run. The aggressive player took the risky pick 16 times out of 20, 80%. The mixed player 11, 55%. The cautious player 3, 15% that spread of styles is personalization. For example, the play-dest notes for your platformer might show one tester always taking the spike path for the bonus coins and another never taking it.

B0701.heard: A chart of the chance of winning on each attempt attempts 1 to 12. Frustration is part of any challenge, but it has to be the kind the player can learn from. The red player learns and wins in about 2.8 attempts. The black player faces an inconsistent game, needs about 10, and learns nothing. For example, missing a jump because you misjudged the gap is frustration you learn from. Missing it because the platform's edge is invisible is not.

B0702.heard: A grid of difficulty against fairness. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is. Fairness means clear expectations and consistent design so the player can learn from failing. The two are separate. Hard and fair is satisfying to win and hard and unfair feels cheap. For example, making the gaps in your level wider raises the difficulty. Hiding a spike under a landing spot with no warning makes the level unfair.

B0801.heard: Bars for how often a skilled player beats a weaker one in this simulated run. Luck and skill are the two things that decide a result, with luck, chance decides. With skill, the player's ability decides and most games mix the two. In Candy Land, all luck, the stronger player wins 50% of the time. For example, a random item from a mystery box is luck while timing a jump over a gap is skill.

B0802.heard: A battle Royale mixes the two with random loot and skilled fights. Chances weighted at 60% and skill at 40 and the skilled player wins 62% of matches. Luck still lets the weaker player win some of the time. For example, a platformer that hands out a random power up at the start of each level, while every jump still takes skill, mixes luck and skill in the same way.

B0803.heard: Counter-strike is mostly skill. Chance is weighted at 30% in skill at 70, and the skilled player wins 86% of matches. These weights are only an illustration. The point is that less luck lets the better player win more often. For example, if testers say your level feels random, put the power-ups in fixed places instead of random ones, so skill decides more of the result.

B0901.heard: A triangle, water beats fire, fire beats grass, grass beats water. Balance means every advantage has a disadvantage, so no roll starts with an unfair edge. Rock paper scissors is one way to get it. Each option beats one and loses to another, so each wins 0.5 against a random opponent. For example, in your game a knight beats an archer, the archer beats a mage, and the mage beats the knight, so no class is best.

B0902.heard: After a change, fire and water now tie. Against a random opponent, fire now wins 0.67 and water drops to 0.33. Fire has an edge with no cost, so the balance is broken and nobody picks water anymore. For example, make the night tie with the mage and the mage loses the one fight it used to win, so players stop choosing it.

B1001.heard: Two rows of turns for four players with player 1 and red. Down time is time a player waits with nothing to do. With turns of 15 seconds, player 1 waits 45 seconds between goes. With turns of 45 seconds, the weight grows to 135. For example, in a mode where two friends take turns at your level, keep each attempt short or give the waiting player something to do.

B1002.heard: Bars for the totals of two six-sided dice, gray for one roll and red for the better of two. Probability is the odds of each result and extra rolls change them. A total of 10 or more comes up 16.7% of the time on one roll and 30.6% with the better of two. For example, if a chest in your level rarely gives a special item, letting the player open it twice makes that item far more likely.

B1101.heard: Four look-alike pairs, difficulty is how hard the opposition is and the dark bar climbs to a hundred. Fairness is whether the player can learn from losing and the red line rises as the player learns. A game can be very hard and still fair.

B1102.heard: A trade-off is giving up one thing to get another. One swap and it is done. Persistence is living with a choice for a set time. The four circles once spent stay spent for the whole stage.

B1103.heard: Luck is when chance decides the result. On the left the skilled players wins, the filled squares come only part of the time. Skill is when the players ability decides it. On the right the skilled player nearly always wins.

B1104.heard: Descriptive play is the game answering an action, a throw, and the box responds at once. Evaluative play is the player asking why the action matters. The chain of boxes runs all the way to the end of the game.

B1201.heard: Each vague request becomes an exact instruction. Make the fights more interesting becomes, give each enemy a different behavior. One charges and one stays back, one can be dodged, and one never misses. Three enemies, three threat levels.

B1202.heard: The shop is too easy to ignore becomes make the choice persist. Robbing the shop sends a shopkeeper to the end of every level. The choice lasts and the shopkeeper waits.

B1203.heard: The game is too random becomes cut luck to 30% with random start loot only and skill deciding most fights. At 60% luck the skilled player wins 62% of matches at 30% 86.

B1204.heard: Waiting for turns is boring becomes, turns average 15 seconds, one roll each and give the other something to do. The wait between turns is 45 seconds, not 135.

B1205.heard: The boss feels unfair becomes same attack, same damage every time so the player can learn it. The red dots jump around between 5 and 40 damage. The dark dots stay at 10 every time.

B1301.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call the choices done. First, does the player see a response to each action and understand why it matters?

B1302.heard: Second is there at least one real trade-off or one lasting choice that stays with the player for a while.

B1303.heard: Third, do different enemies or options call for different answers. That is unit differentiation, and it is one thing that makes a situational choice possible.

B1304.heard: Fourth is the challenge hard and fair so that failing teaches something. The difficulty can be high as long as the fairness holds.

B1305.heard: Fifth is the mix of luck and skill right for this game. More luck lets weaker players win and more skill rewards practice.

B1306.heard: Sixth is every option worth taking and our turns short enough to keep downtime low, then say it exactly, not make fights interesting but one enemy never misses.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, descriptive play shows a response and evaluative play asks why it matters. Risk versus reward pays more for the harder riskier action. A trade-off is one swap and persistence makes a choice stick for a set time. Situational choice depends on the moment, personalization on the player's style. Difficulty is how hard it is and fairness is whether you can learn from losing. Rock paper scissors keeps options balanced and short turns keep downtime low.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game design terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use descriptive play, evaluative play agency, risk versus reward, trade-off, persistence, situational choice, personalization, difficulty and fairness. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms choices and challenge at Nick Bear Brown.
